diet without significant distention.   His pain was well
controlled.  His stool output had decreased to approximately
600 cc per day.  The patient was able to be discharged to
home.

wean, and concern of bronchopleural fistula.

a pneumonia that was believed to have progressed despite
treatment with ceftriaxone and azithromycin.  The patient was
subsequently placed on a regimen of ciprofloxacin and
vancomycin.  The patient had also been placed on a steroid
taper for his chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.  He had
required large amounts of benzodiazepines at the outside
hospital and was thought to have been experiencing alcohol
withdrawal.  The patient had persistent tachycardia at the
outside hospital and been ruled out for myocardial infarction
by enzymes.  He was, however, suspected to have had some
degree of demand ischemia.

 1.  Severe bolus chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with

10.  Hypercholesterolemia.

extensive smoking history.  The patient has a history of
alcohol abuse with a history of withdrawal.

a ventilator which was set at IMV with a volume of 800, a
rate of 12, inspired oxygen of 50%, and a pressure support

respiratory rate of 13, and oxygen saturation of 94%.

apparent distress.  He was ventilated and sedated.  HEENT
revealed pupils that were equally, round, and reactive to
light.  An orogastric tube was in place.  On neck
examination, the patient had no cervical lymphadenopathy.  On
cardiac examination, the patient had a regular rate and
rhythm with a normal S1 and S2, and no murmur, rubs or
gallops.  On pulmonary examination, the patient had crepitus
along his right chest wall with a chest tube in his right
thoracic wall.  Coarse wheezes were heard bilaterally.  On
abdominal examination, the patient's belly was soft,
nontender, and nondistended, with normal bowel sounds.
Extremity examination revealed no edema.  Vascular
examination revealed good capillary refill.  For access, the
patient had a right peripherally inserted central catheter
line in place.

PERTINENT LABORATORY DATA ON ADMISSION:  The patient had a
white blood cell count of 14.5, hematocrit of 38.8, platelets
of 233.  His Chem-7 revealed a sodium of 138, potassium
of 4.3, chloride of 96, bicarbonate of 30, BUN of 21, and
creatinine of 0.8, with a glucose of 127.  His ALT was 44,
with an AST of 26, and alkaline phosphatase of 77, and a
total bilirubin of 0.7.

RADIOLOGY/IMAGING:   Electrocardiogram revealed a normal
sinus rhythm with a rate of 65, normal axis, normal channels,
normal intervals.  ST elevations in II, III, and F with no Q
waves appreciated, and an inverted T wave in aVL.  When this
was compared to his admission electrocardiogram at the
outside hospital there appeared to be no changes.

Chest x-ray revealed chest tube in the right chest with a
small residual right pneumothorax, left lower lobe opacity,
and a question of a left pleural effusion were noted.

HOSPITAL COURSE:   This patient was directly admitted to [**Hospital1 1444**] Medical Intensive Care Unit
on [**2148-10-17**], from the outside hospital.  The
patient presented febrile with an elevated white count with
an oxygen saturation of 94% on the above vent settings with
coarse rhonchorous breath sounds, right chest wall crepitus,
and a chest x-ray significant for right pneumothorax.

Cardiothoracic Surgery was consulted and replaced the
patient's chest tube.  The patient completed his steroid
taper and was placed on an antibiotic regimen of
levofloxacin, gentamicin, and vancomycin.  Flagyl was
subsequently added for anaerobic coverage after an episode of
succulent nasogastric aspirate.  A KUB performed revealed no
obstruction.  The patient continued to spike fevers, and his
regimen was changed to ceftazidime, vancomycin, and Flagyl to
cover possible ventilator associated pneumonia.  The patient
had transient episodes of hypotension unresponsive fluid
boluses, requiring short intervals on pressors.  The patient
eventually defervesced for 48 hours.  A repeat chest CT
revealed severe bolus disease with a large left bola under
tension and bilateral pneumonia.

On [**10-22**], the patient had an arterial blood gas that
revealed hypoxemia.  PEEP 5 mmHg was added with modest
improvement in the PAO2.  On [**10-24**], the patient spiked
a temperature to 100.9.  The patient was pan cultured with no
growth on any cultures.  He was diuresed with modest
improvement in oxygenation.  By [**10-24**], all of his
access lines had been changed.  The patient continued to
spike temperatures to 101 to 102.  Stool studies were
negative including studies for Clostridium difficile toxin.
On [**10-24**], the patient had a tracheostomy placed, and
on [**10-25**], the patient underwent a PEG-J placement by
Interventional Radiology.  On [**10-26**], the patient
continued to be hypoxemic.  The concern at that point was for
right-to-left shunt secondary to the patient's bilateral
pneumonia or pulmonary embolus.  A CT angiogram revealed a
large left [**MD Number(3) 26547**] pulmonary embolism, and the patient's
chest tube in an intraparenchymal location.  The chest tube
was pulled by Cardiothoracic Surgery, and the patient was
started on a continuous heparin infusion.  An echocardiogram
was performed to evaluate right ventricular function but was
severely limited by the patient's bolus disease.

On [**10-29**], the patient became markedly hypoxemic with
an emergent CT that revealed 50% recurrent pneumothorax on
the right.  Cardiothoracic Surgery placed a right chest tube
with resolution of the pneumothorax.  However, the patient
required paralysis in order to achieve cooperation with the
ventilator.  That evening, the patient became markedly
hypotensive requiring Neo-Synephrine support.  An
electrocardiogram and chest x-ray done at that time were
unremarkable.

A family meeting was held the next day, and the patient was
made do not resuscitate.  The patient was eventually weaned
off pressors.  The patient remained hypercarbic and
relatively hypoxemic.  The patient was eventually placed on
pressure control ventilation, and his I to E ratio was
altered to improve oxygenation.  The patient's driving
pressure and PEEP were also increased.  On [**10-31**], the
patient completed a 10-day course of antibiotics and all were
discontinued.  The patient was re-cultured.  By [**10-31**],
all of his access lines had been relocated for a second time.
His Foley was changed.

On [**11-1**], the patient became markedly acidotic,
hypercarbic, and hypoxemic.  His ventilatory settings were
adjusted.  A conversation was held with the patient's
daughter who expressed her desire to have the patient
designated comfort measures only.  Multiple attempts to
contact the rest of the patient's family had been
unsuccessful.  Ultimately, on [**2148-11-3**], at
8:27 p.m, the patient expired.

CONDITION AT DISCHARGE:  Expired.

DISCHARGE STATUS:  The patient expired on [**2148-11-3**],
at 8:27 p.m.

not recover.  The patient was declared dead in the operating

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:  The patient is an 87 year old
woman who was found by her family in her bedroom, which is in
a closet.  She was seen at that time to have a left facial
droop and not moving her left arm.

The patient was vomiting on arrival and not speaking.
Because there was a bottle of Drano with her when she was
found, there was a question of Drano ingestion and she was
intubated in the Emergency Room.  However, she got a
nasogastric lavage and had no blood and no burns on her face.
She was guaiac negative as well.

By CT scan, the patient was found at that time to have a
large right middle cerebral artery stroke, no bleeding, and
also to be in atrial fibrillation.  When she first came in,
she was mumbling and she was last seen by her family the day
prior to admission at around 5:30 p.m.  She was found at 8:30
p.m. on the day of admission.  At baseline, the patient lives
alone and is reportedly a high functioning individual.  She
pays her own bills and does her own shopping.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:  Cataracts, no primary care physician,
[**Name10 (NameIs) **] diabetes.

MEDICATIONS ON ADMISSION:  None.

ALLERGIES:  The patient has no known drug allergies.

FAMILY HISTORY:  Noncontributory; no cardiac history.

SOCIAL HISTORY:  The patient does not smoke and drinks
alcohol occasionally.  She lives independently by herself,
with her grandchildren involved in her life.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:  On physical examination on admission,
the patient had a pulse of 61, blood pressure 150 and
temperature 102.  She was intubated and sedated, not
responsive, no purposeful movement.  She could doll pass
midline, pupils were 1 mm bilaterally, slightly reactive,
corneal intact right eye, no corneal on left, unable to
determine facial symmetric since she was intubated.  Motor:
Reportedly moving right side prior to intubation, slight
movement on left leg observed, left arm flaccid.  Sensory:
Withdrew left leg to pain, otherwise inconsistently
responsive.  Reflexes:  Left toe was upgoing.

tract infection as seen by urinalysis.  Blood cultures and
urine cultures were sent.  A complete blood count and Chem-7
were all unremarkable.

HOSPITAL COURSE:  The patient was admitted to the Neurologic
Intensive Care Unit because of her stroke.  She was started
on aspirin and it was elected not to anticoagulate her since
the size of her stroke would have substantial risk of
bleeding on heparin.  Her blood pressure was kept between 140
and 160 and it was thought that the etiology of the stroke
was atrial fibrillation.  In addition, she was started on
mannitol to control swelling and, also, her fever was
aggressively controlled with Tylenol as well as having
aggressive blood sugar control.

On admission, the patient had a high glucose, which
continued, and an insulin drip was started.  She was hydrated
with intravenous fluids and kept intubated.  She ruled out
for a myocardial infarction with negative CKs.  Mannitol was
continued.  Her urinary tract infection was treated with
antibiotics.

The patient was febrile persistently on [**2109-2-9**].
She had a fever workup, including chest x-ray and blood and
urine cultures were sent.  No source for fever was identified
other than the urinary tract infection, which was already
being treated.

The insulin drip was discontinued on [**2109-2-9**] and the
patient did well on subcutaneous insulin.  She was also
extubated on this day without difficulty and they planned to
transfer the patient out of the unit on [**2109-2-10**].
However, there was no bed available on the floor.

At that time, the patient's neurologic examination showed her
to be awake, in no acute distress; did not open eyes
spontaneously or to command.  She moved her right side
spontaneously.  She was able to lift her right arm and wiggle
her toes.  She was nonverbal.  Pupils were equal and reacting
without tracking.  Face was symmetric.  Decreased tone on the
left, no anti-gravity on the left.  Triple flexion on the
left with pain.  Slightly decreased deep tendon reflexes on
the left.

Tube feeds were started.  The patient then had epistaxis and
bleeding from her oral cavity.  Otolaryngology was contact[**Name (NI) **]
and they found two active bleeding sites on the left nasal
septum, one anterior caudal, one superior, also an abraded
area on the right inferior turbinate oozing slightly,
positive nasogastric tube on the right; all bleeding sites
cauterized, with good hemostasis.  She also had soft palate
lacerations, likely secondary to intubation, which were
healing well.  After that, she had no problems with bleeding.

The patient was finally transferred out on the floor on
[**2109-2-13**].  A follow-up head CT scan was obtained at
that time.  The CT scan showed evolving near total right
middle cerebral artery infarction, greatly increased in size,
now associated with significant mass effect and slight
herniation of the uncus.

The patient was, at that time, started on oral glycerol for
the mass effect but then, on further discussion with the
stroke team, it was determined that her clinical status had
not changed and the oral glycerol was stopped after three
doses, without any adverse effect.

After further discussion with the patient's family, they
decided that they wanted the patient to be able to have means
of obtaining nutrition and, because of her mental status, she
would not be able to eat on her own.  Thus, a
gastrojejunostomy tube was placed on [**2109-2-15**].  She
will be continued on tube feeds via gastrostomy tube.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
Regular insulin sliding scale.
Aspirin 325 per G-tube q.d.
Heparin 5,000 units s.c.b.i.d.
Zantac 150 mg per G-tube b.i.d.
Lopressor 50 mg per G-tube t.i.d., hold for systolic blood
pressure less than 130 and heart rate less than 55.
Tube feeds.
NPH insulin 20 units s.c.b.i.d. while tube feeds are going
and cut in half when patient is NPO.
Levaquin 250 mg per G-tube q.d. through [**2109-2-18**].

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:
1.  Large right middle cerebral artery stroke.
2.  Atrial fibrillation, not on anticoagulation because of
    risk of bleeding.

 FINDINGS:  On the diffusion images, no evidence of an area of restricted
 diffusion is identified to indicate acute infarct or evidence of encephalitis.
 Subtle areas of increased signal on FLAIR axial images bilaterally in the
 lateral portions of the temporal lobes which could be artifacts from
 pulsation. These areas are not seen on T2 weighted images.

 within the brain.  Following gadolinium, subtle meningeal enhancement is

 finding.  No distinct parenchymal enhancement is seen.

 There is a fluid level with soft tissue changes in the sphenoid sinus.

 IMPRESSION:

 nonspecific finding and could be related to the recent lumbar puncture.  No
 evidence of intrinsic enhancement seen within the brain.

 2.  No evidence of restricted diffusion on diffusion weighted images to
 indicate infarct or encephalitis.

 3.  Subtle areas of signal abnormalities bilaterally along the lateral aspect
 of the temporal lobes could be artifactual secondary to pulsation - these
 sites are not typical for the appearance of encephalitis.  However, if there
 continues to be clinical suspicion of a herpes encephalitis, repeat coronal T2
 and FLAIR images can confirm this finding.

 4.  No evidence of hydrocephalus, mass effect, hemorrhage, or territorial
 infarct.

confirmed the "Do Not Resuscitate" status from prior
discussions and the patient expired at 10 a.m. on [**1-28**].
